Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is an additive manufacturing technology that was invented by Scott Crump in the 1980s and is now used widely in 3D printing.
Facts.Fact 2: The FDM process involves melting a thermoplastic filament, which is then extruded through a nozzle to build the object layer by layer.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM can utilize various types of materials, including ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene), PLA (polylactic acid), and PEEK (polyether ether ketone), each having unique characteristics suitable for different applications.
Facts.Fact 4: One of the advantages of FDM is its capacity to print complex geometries and cavities. Support structures made from soluble material are used for overhanging parts and can be easily removed post-printing.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM provides a good balance between dimensional accuracy and resolution, with accuracy typically around ± 0.5% and resolution from 0.1 to 0.3 mm.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM technology is widely used for prototyping due to its relatively low cost and fast turnaround time compared to traditional manufacturing methods such as injection molding.
Facts.Fact 7: Despite many advantages, FDM has some limitations such as problems with layer adhesion resulting in weaknesses along the Z-axis, meaning parts printed horizontally are typically stronger than those printed vertically.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM is also used in bio-fabrication where living cells are used as printing material to produce living tissues or organs for medical applications.
Facts.Fact 9: The surface finish in FDM printed parts can be rough due to the layer-by-layer process, often requiring post-processing steps like sanding or filling to achieve a smooth finish.
Facts.Fact 10: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a green technology as it generates minimal waste, mainly uses recyclable materials, and can adopt a decentralized manufacturing model reducing transportation emissions.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is an additive manufacturing technology commonly used for modeling, prototyping, and production applications.
Facts.Fact 2: The FDM technology was developed by Scott Crump in the 1980s and commercialized by Stratasys Ltd., which still holds its principal patents.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM works on an 'additive' principle by laying down material in layers; hence it is also known as an additive manufacturing process.
Facts.Fact 4: It uses a thermoplastic filament, which is heated to its melting point and then extruded through a nozzle layer-by-layer to build an object.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM is capable of 3D printing complex parts with a high degree of accuracy and durability, making it widely used in industries such as automotive, aerospace, and healthcare.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM utilizes a variety of materials like ABS, PLA, PETG, and other thermoplastic polymers, each providing different strengths, flexibility, and temperature resistances.
Facts.Fact 7: The FDM process commonly involves three stages: pre-processing (or slicing), production (or layer-by-layer construction), and post-processing (removal of support materials and finishing).
Facts.Fact 8: One crucial advantage of FDM technology is that it allows for extensive material selection and design flexibility, including integration of multiple colours and materials within the same print.
Facts.Fact 9: Challenges with FDM can include issues with layer separation, warping, and variability across different machines, which impact the consistency and quality of printed objects.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM is becoming more ubiquitous as a technology, not only in industrial applications but also personal, due to the affordability of desktop FDM printers.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is an additive manufacturing technique that works by depositing material in layers, building up a product from the ground up.
Facts.Fact 2: FDM uses a thermoplastic filament, which is heated to its melting point and then extruded, layer by layer, to create a three-dimensional object.
Facts.Fact 3: The FDM technique is commonly applied in rapid prototyping, production parts, and concept modeling, due to its flexibility in materials and design capabilities.
Facts.Fact 4: FDM is guided by a computer-aided design (CAD) software. The design is sliced into layers by the software and the printer follows the design to create the object from the bottom up.
Facts.Fact 5: One of the key principles of FDM is its layer-by-layer manufacturing process. This process allows the creation of complex geometries and internal structures that would be difficult with traditional manufacturing methods.
Facts.Fact 6: The nozzle in FDM can move in both horizontal and vertical directions, which allows it to create different shapes and structures with high precision.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM can work with a variety of materials such as ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene), PLA (Polylactic Acid), PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol), and more advanced composites with embedded materials.
Facts.Fact 8: The strength of an object created through FDM can differ in the vertical and horizontal directions due to its layer-by-layer construction. This is a phenomenon known as anisotropy.
Facts.Fact 9: Support structures are essential in FDM process when creating overhangs and undercuts. These are removed post-production once the object has cooled and solidified.
Facts.Fact 10: Accuracy and resolution in FDM is determined by several factors including layer height, nozzle diameter, and the precision of the machine's movements. Smaller layer height and nozzle diameter result in higher detail but increase the time for printing.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is extensively utilized in fields such as aerospace engineering because it permits the production of lightweight, functional prototypes and end-use parts with advanced geometries.
Facts.Fact 2: In the medical field, FDM has been employed to produce custom prosthetics, implants and anatomical models for surgical planning, due to its ability to create personalized and biocompatible components.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM is largely used in the automotive industry. This technology has allowed for the production of complex parts such as fixtures, jigs and other manufacturing aids that significantly reduce costs and improve performance.
Facts.Fact 4: Education and research institutions frequently use FDM for teaching purposes and prototype development. The technology’s accessibility and ease of use make it an ideal learning tool for students and professionals alike.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM technology is used in the construction industry as it enables the production of scale models, architectural prototypes, and even 3D printed buildings with a high level of accuracy and detail.
Facts.Fact 6: Fashion and art industries have been revolutionized by FDM, which allows the creation of intricate designs, apparel, and sculptures that were once considered impossible or too expensive to manufacture.
Facts.Fact 7: In the food industry, FDM has been employed in the production of food-safe items such as cookie cutters, custom molds, and other specialty tools due to its ability to work with FDA-approved materials.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM is extensively used in the creation of custom electronics encasing, cable management solutions, and cooling fan ducts, due to its capability of producing components that can withstand heat and mechanical stress.
Facts.Fact 9: In the field of robotics, FDM plays a significant role as it enables the fabrication of parts with unique shapes and various mechanical properties, such as robot chassis, gears, joints, and sensor mounts.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM is notably used in the entertainment industry for the creation of props, costumes, and detailed set models. It allows the production of items with a wide range of colors, materials, and finishes, contributing to more realistic and immersive experiences.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a cost-effective 3D printing method. The materials used in FDM are less expensive compared to those used in other 3D printing technologies.
Facts.Fact 2: FDM allows the use of a wide range of thermoplastic materials, including ABS, PLA, and Nylon, among others. This means it can produce objects with different physical properties, such as flexibility and strength.
Facts.Fact 3: Unlike some other 3D printing techniques that require the usage of support materials which are different from the primary material, FDM uses the same material for both object and support structure, simplifying the post-processing steps.
Facts.Fact 4: FDM technology is capable of creating complex geometric shapes that might be hard to achieve with traditional manufacturing methods.
Facts.Fact 5: In FDM, the layer-by-layer method allows for the inclusion of internal features that couldn't be placed in a part using subtractive manufacturing processes.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM has a relatively low learning curve compared to other 3D printing technologies, given its straightforward process, and is therefore more accessible for beginners or educational settings.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM is excellent for rapid prototyping because it can quickly and inexpensively produce prototypes directly from digital models.
Facts.Fact 8: Since FDM can use biodegradable materials like PLA, it can be more environmentally friendly compared to other 3D printing techniques.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM 3D printing does not often require much post-processing of completed parts. This can save manufacturers valuable time and resources.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM machines generally have a large build volume, making them suitable for creating larger parts or multiple parts simultaneously.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling has limitations in terms of precision; the process often produces lower resolution models than other types of 3D printing methods, such as stereolithography (SLA) or selective laser sintering (SLS).
Facts.Fact 2: Some materials used in FDM, like thermoplastics, can warp during cooling, limiting the process's capacity to accurately reproduce models.
Facts.Fact 3: Fused deposition modeling can struggle with producing complex geometries, such as sharp edges and intricate details. Overhangs and undercuts are particularly difficult as they may require support structures that need to be removed post-production.
Facts.Fact 4: The speed of fused deposition modeling is relatively slow, especially when creating large, solid models. This could limit its utility for rapid prototyping or mass production.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM has limitations in the variety of materials it can use. It generally relies on thermoplastic filaments, making it less versatile than other 3D printing methods that can handle a wider array of materials.
Facts.Fact 6: The material strength of FDM output is often unidirectional, meaning the final pieces can be weaker in one direction and more susceptible to breakage.
Facts.Fact 7: Due to the way FDM builds up layers, there may be visible step lines on the final object, limiting its aesthetic potential without post-processing.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM has temperature limitations. Using certain high-performance materials may require the use of a heated build chamber, which not all FDM printers have.
Facts.Fact 9: Some FDM machines have size limitations, not allowing larger objects to be printed in one piece. This requires the object to be divided into separate parts, printed individually and later assembled.
Facts.Fact 10: Although FDM is known for enabling in-house printing and reducing costs, it could still be expensive in terms of energy use and materials, especially when printing large volumes or complex features that need extensive support structures.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is a type of additive manufacturing technology that involves using a plastic filament or metal wire that's fed from a coil, providing precise layer-by-layer construction.
Facts.Fact 2: FDM printers apply heat at two stages: first at the extrusion head that melts the material, and second, in the build chamber that keeps the entire model uniformly warm to prevent deformation.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM technology uses a variety of materials: ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene), PLA (Polylactic Acid), PPSF (Polyphenylsulfone), polycarbonate, and others, catering to different strength and flexibility requirements.
Facts.Fact 4: Modern FDM printers have dual extrusion capabilities, allowing for the printing of complex models with multiple colors or materials in a single print.
Facts.Fact 5: Inside an FDM printer, there's a 'Y-E' motion system which moves the extrusion head in the X and Y-axes and the build platform in the Z-axis, ensuring high-precision movements.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM uses slicing software to interpret 3D modeling data and translate it into a format the printer can understand. This software determines the path the extruder should follow, the material type and the layer thickness among other parameters.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM printers use support structures to handle overhangs and cavities during the printing process. These structures are made of the same or different material (that can be dissolved or broken away) and are removed after printing.
Facts.Fact 8: Some FDM printers are equipped with heated build plates to enhance adhesion during the print, prevent warping and enable easier removal of the completed object from the build platform.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM can print with dissolvable support material that can be removed in a water or chemical bath post fabrication, a key feature that enables the creation of complex geometric structures.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM technology has seen advancements like automatic bed leveling and calibration, which enhance print quality by ensuring the initial layer sticks properly and that each subsequent layer is deposited accurately.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) produces minimal waste as compared to traditional manufacturing methods, as it’s an additive process that only uses material necessary for the finished product.
Facts.Fact 2: The use of thermoplastics in FDM, which are recyclable, contributes to a reduction in environmental impacts.
Facts.Fact 3: While the manufacturing process of FDM is less wasteful, the energy consumption of the machines can be quite high, potentially leading to increased carbon footprints.
Facts.Fact 4: The narrow range of materials usable by FDM may limit the ability of companies to choose environmentally-friendly material options.
Facts.Fact 5: The biodegradable plastic PLA, frequently used in FDM, can contribute to microplastic pollution if not disposed of properly due to its lack of industrial compost facilities.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM machines must reach high temperatures to melt the thermoplastic filament, which can potentially release harmful VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds) impacting air quality.
Facts.Fact 7: The lifespan of FDM 3D printed objects can be shorter than traditionally manufactured products, possibly leading to earlier disposal and increased waste.
Facts.Fact 8: Mass production through FDM can pose environmental challenges, as the energy use and waste production can scale upward significantly with volume.
Facts.Fact 9: The acoustic pollution from FDM printers is an often overlooked negative environmental impact, as many FDM machines produce notable noise pollution.
Facts.Fact 10: Development of more energy-efficient FDM printers and the use of renewable energy sources can help mitigate some of the environmental impacts of this manufacturing method.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), also known as Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF), is an additive manufacturing technique that uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material.
Facts.Fact 2: The technique was developed by Scott Crump in the late 1980s and then commercially developed by Stratasys Ltd in the 1990s.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM works on an 'additive' principle by laying down material in layers; a plastic filament or metal wire is unwound from a coil and supplied to produce a part.
Facts.Fact 4: The filament is heated at a temperature below its melting point to make it flexible, then further heated upon deposition to bond with the layer beneath, creating a solid structure.
Facts.Fact 5: In FDM, one of the key advantages is the ability to print in different materials. This includes ABS, PLA, PEEK, and other thermoplastic polymers, giving a wide range of functional properties.
Facts.Fact 6: Friendly to beginners and professionals alike, the FDM process is known for its simplicity, reliability, and vast array of available materials.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM is a well-suited technique for producing models, prototypes, production parts and even for rapid tooling applications due to its compatibility with various thermoplastics.
Facts.Fact 8: This additive manufacturing technology can print complex geometries and cavities that may not be possible with traditional subtractive or formative manufacturing processes.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM is an environmentally friendly 3D printing process, as it uses thermoplastics which can be recycled, and there's minimal waste as the technology supports precise, on-demand production.
Facts.Fact 10: Despite its advantages, FDM has limitations including lower resolution and finish quality compared to other 3D printing methods, as well as lower strength and rigidity in the Z direction due to layer adhesion.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was invented by an American engineer named Scott Crump in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: Crump, the co-founder of Stratasys Ltd., patented this technology in 1989. The patent covered a 'plastic jet apparatus for three-dimensional printing'
Facts.Fact 3: Fused Deposition Modeling, as an additive manufacturing technology, gradually developed in the 1990s after the patent was approved.
Facts.Fact 4: In the early days, Stratasys utilized ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene) plastic as the primary raw material for FDM process.
Facts.Fact 5: The FDM patent held by Stratasys expired in 2009, which allowed other companies to exploit and innovate upon this technology.
Facts.Fact 6: Post-expiration of the patent, FDM came to be widely adopted due to its low cost and ease of implementation, leading to the surge of desktop 3D printing.
Facts.Fact 7: The term 'FDM' is trademarked by Stratasys, so other companies using the same technology often use the term 'Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF)' instead.
Facts.Fact 8: The progress in material science in the 21st century enhanced the versatility of FDM, expanding its utility beyond ABS to other materials such as Nylon, ASA, PLA, PETG, and more.
Facts.Fact 9: The refinement of FDM technology has also allowed for the printing of composite materials, combining plastic with other substances like wood, metal, or carbon fiber.
Facts.Fact 10: In its early years, FDM was used primarily for prototyping. However, with advancements in technology and materials, it's now used for the production of end-use parts in industries like aerospace, medicine, and automotive.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) technology was developed by Scott Crump in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: The first commercial FDM machine was released in 1992 by the company Stratasys, co-founded by Scott Crump.
Facts.Fact 3: The development of FDM was rooted in the goal of creating a more affordable, accessible, and practical solution for rapid prototyping.
Facts.Fact 4: Crump's FDM innovation marked a significant shift in 3D printing, transitioning it from a concept to a practical tool for engineerings and designers.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM technology led to a drastic reduction in the time and cost of prototype development, significantly impacting various manufacturing industries.
Facts.Fact 6: Throughout its development, FDM has evolved to be compatible not only with thermoplastics, but also with a variety of other materials such as ceramics and metals.
Facts.Fact 7: Stratasys's patented FDM process originally involved the use of two materials - one for the model and another that forms support structures which are removed post-printing.
Facts.Fact 8: Further developments in FDM technology have enabled the use of soluble supports, allowing for complex geometries to be printed with greater ease and precision.
Facts.Fact 9: The development of FDM technology has kept pace with digital control systems, enabling higher precision, repeatability, and control of the printing process.
Facts.Fact 10: In 2009, after the Stratasys patent expired, the FDM technology exploded in popularity, significantly contributing to the rise of affordable consumer-grade 3D printing.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was developed by S. Scott Crump in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: The patent for FDM technology was filed by Crump in 1989, marking an important milestone in its history.
Facts.Fact 3: Crump co-founded the company Stratasys Ltd. in 1989, which played a pivotal role in introducing the FDM technology to the commercial market.
Facts.Fact 4: In 1992, Stratasys sold its first FDM machine, the 3D Modeler.
Facts.Fact 5: The FDM patent came off the 'patent cliff' and into the public domain in 2009, enabling rapid technological and market development of FDM 3D printers.
Facts.Fact 6: The expiration of the FDM patent led to a surge in the development of affordable desktop FDM 3D printers, a key milestone in democratizing 3D printing technology.
Facts.Fact 7: In 2012, Stratasys merged with 3D printing company Objet to become a major player in both FDM and PolyJet technologies.
Facts.Fact 8: In 2014, Stratasys revealed the first triple-jetting 3D printer system, further expanding the capabilities of FDM technology.
Facts.Fact 9: 2015 marked a key milestone when General Electric announced they would use FDM technology to 3D print fuel nozzles for its LEAP aircraft engines, marking a major industrial application.
Facts.Fact 10: As of 2019, FDM remains the most widely used 3D printing technology, reflecting its significant development and impact since its introduction over 30 years ago.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a proprietary system developed by Stratasys Ltd., a leading manufacturer of 3D printers.
Facts.Fact 2: Under this proprietary system, thermoplastic filament gets heated to their melting point and then extruded, layer by layer, to create a three-dimensional object.
Facts.Fact 3: Stratasys Ltd holds various patents related to FDM technology, restricting other companies to use similar technology under different names such as Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF).
Facts.Fact 4: Unlike other 3D printing technologies, FDM creates objects that can withstand heat, chemical exposure, or mechanical stress, given its use of industrial-grade, high-performance thermoplastics.
Facts.Fact 5: The proprietary FDM system can utilize ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene) plastic, polycarbonate, PPSF (Polyphenylsulfone), and other advanced materials in the 3D printing process.
Facts.Fact 6: The use of multiple materials and colors in a single print cycle is one feature of the FDM technology under the proprietary system.
Facts.Fact 7: Under Stratasys' system, FDM produces fewer toxic fumes during printing as compared to other 3D printing technologies, making it safer for use in office or home settings.
Facts.Fact 8: Stratasys also provides proprietary, easy-to-remove support structures that allow for intricate design capabilities in FDM 3D printing.
Facts.Fact 9: Stratasys offers FDM 3D printers in a range of sizes and price points, enabling its use for both industrial applications and smaller, consumer-focused applications.
Facts.Fact 10: In the proprietary system of Stratasys, constant innovations are made in the area of software, materials, and hardware to improve and expand the capabilities of FDM technology.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a type of additive manufacturing technology that falls under the category of material extrusion. It's different from methods like Stereolithography (SLA) and Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) that fall under vat photopolymerization and powder bed fusion categories respectively.
Facts.Fact 2: Compared to other methods such as Selective Laser Melting (SLM) or Electron Beam Melting (EBM), FDM doesn't require a high-powered laser or electron beam, making the machines safer and less expensive.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM has a more limited range of materials it can use compared to methods such as SLS or SLA. Common FDM materials include thermoplastics like ABS and PLA, whereas other methods may utilize metals, ceramics, and other durable materials.
Facts.Fact 4: One of the major differences between FDM and other methods like SLA is the finish quality. FDM often has visible layer lines, whereas SLA can produce parts with smooth finish which are close to injection molded parts.
Facts.Fact 5: Compared to methods such as Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS), FDM has much lower accuracy and resolution. This may limit its use in applications where precise dimensional accuracy is required.
Facts.Fact 6: Unlike other methods such as SLS or SLM, FDM doesn't require support structures to be removed in a separate post-processing step. The support structures in FDM are usually made from soluble materials that can be washed away.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM machines are generally simpler and more reliable than machines for other methods. This is partly because they have fewer moving parts and don't require powdered materials, which can be difficult to handle safely.
Facts.Fact 8: In terms of working principle, FDM builds an object layer by layer from the bottom up by heating and extruding thermoplastic filament, a method contrastingly different from Direct Metal Laser Sintering that fuses metal powder layer by layer using a high powered laser.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM technology typically has a slower production speed than most other 3D printing methods such as SLA and SLS, making it less suitable for mass production applications.
Facts.Fact 10: SLA and FDM differ also in the way they create parts. While FDM heats and extrudes filament, SLA uses a laser to cure a resin, resulting in differences in strength of finished parts, with FDM parts generally being stronger than SLA parts.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) technology was invented by S. Scott Crump in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: The patent application for FDM technology was filed in the United States in 1989.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM technology was commercialized in the early 1990s by Stratasys Ltd, a company that Crump co-founded with his wife Lisa Crump.
Facts.Fact 4: Originally, fused deposition modeling primarily used two types of materials: wax and thermoplastics.
Facts.Fact 5: In 2005, Stratasys introduced a new FDM system capable of printing in high-performance engineering thermoplastics, greatly expanding the technology's capabilities.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM technology became more popular after 2009 when the original patents held by Stratasys expired, allowing other companies to develop similar technologies.
Facts.Fact 7: The expiration of the patent also led to the proliferation of low-cost FDM 3D printers, making the technology accessible for individual consumers and small businesses.
Facts.Fact 8: Despite the expiration of the original patent, Stratasys continued to hold proprietary rights over several key aspects of FDM technology, including some hardware and software elements.
Facts.Fact 9: The advancements in FDM have enabled the use of a wide range of plastic filaments including ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene), PLA (Polylactic Acid), Nylon, PET (Polyethylene terephthalate), and more.
Facts.Fact 10: Today, FDM is one of the most commonly used additive manufacturing methods and has found applications in a variety of sectors, including aerospace, automotive, medical, and many others.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) technology was developed by Scott Crump in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: Scott Crump invented FDM technology in his home and initially used a mixture of candle wax and polymer for making models.
Facts.Fact 3: In 1988, Scott Crump filed a patent for FDM technology which was later granted in 1992.
Facts.Fact 4: Following the invention and patenting, Crump together with his wife Lisa Crump founded Stratasys Ltd. in 1989.
Facts.Fact 5: Stratasys Ltd, headquartered in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, was specifically founded to commercialize FDM technology.
Facts.Fact 6: The first commercial FDM 3D printer, the '3D Modeler', was released by Stratasys in 1991, three years after the company was founded.
Facts.Fact 7: Over time, Stratasys made numerous updates to FDM technology including precision improvements, speed enhancements, and capability of using different materials.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM technology in its early inception utilizes two materials. One to create the model and the other temporary material for support which can be dissolved in water.
Facts.Fact 9: Originating from a small niche, FDM has become one of the most common 3D printing technologies used globally, even outside of industrial contexts.
Facts.Fact 10: Despite the patent expiring in 2009, Stratasys continues to remain a significant player in the 3D printing industry, thanks to the strong foundation laid during FDM's inception.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was invented by S. Scott Crump in the late 1980s.

Facts.Fact 3: Scott Crump patented the FDM technology in the U.S. in 1989 under the name 'Apparatus and method for creating three-dimensional objects'.
Facts.Fact 4: In 1992, Scott and his wife Lisa Crump co-founded Stratasys Ltd., in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, which is now one of the world's leading 3D printing companies.

Facts.Fact 8: Initial tests in FDM development were done using standard ABS plastic, which is still commonly used in FDM processes today.
Facts.Fact 9: From the outset, the aim of the research was to create a 3D printing technique that was both practical and accessible in manufacturing and prototyping.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was first developed by S. Scott Crump in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: In 1988, Crump formed the company Stratasys Ltd., to commercialize his invention.
Facts.Fact 3: The first patented device capable of FDM was named '3D Modeler', filed in 1989 by Crump.
Facts.Fact 4: Stratasys introduced the first industrial-grade FDM machine, the '3D Modeler', in 1992.
Facts.Fact 5: In the early machines, thermoplastic materials were used, which were dispensed by an extrusion nozzle which was controlled by a computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) software package.
Facts.Fact 6: The first machines fabricated models in a layer-by-layer fashion, with each layer adhering to the layer below it, forming a three-dimensional object.
Facts.Fact 7: These early FDM machines were primarily used for rapid prototyping, significantly reducing the time and cost associated with the production of prototypes.
Facts.Fact 8: Original FDM machines had limitations in terms of the complexity of geometries that could be produced due to issues of support for the layers during the extrusion process.
Facts.Fact 9: Stratasys released major upgrades to FDM machines over time, focusing on enhancing precision, ease of use, and client-specific customization options with the introduction of new software and hardware features.
Facts.Fact 10: By the late 1990s and early 2000s, FDM technologies were incorporated into a wide range of industries, including automotive, aerospace, and medical fields, signifying the widespread utilization of these first-generation machines.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was developed by Scott Crump in the late 1980s. He patented the technology in 1989.
Facts.Fact 2: The original patent granted for FDM was U.S. Patent No. 5,121,329, filed on May 24, 1990 and issued on June 9, 1992.
Facts.Fact 3: Crump co-founded the company Stratasys Ltd. in 1988 to commercialize the FDM patent.
Facts.Fact 4: Scott Crump's patent covered the process of forming a three-dimensional physical object by depositing material in layers upon one another.
Facts.Fact 5: The patent described the use of thermoplastics as a filament material which is heated to a semi-liquid state and then extruded through a nozzle.
Facts.Fact 6: Later patents, such as the U.S. Patent No. 6,004,124, expanded the process to include the use of 'multiple, differentiable filaments' to make multi-material and multi-color objects.
Facts.Fact 7: The original patent expired in June 2009, which effectively opened up the market for third-party FDM printers.
Facts.Fact 8: Even after the expiration of the original FDM patent, Stratasys still holds numerous patents related to improvements and variations of the technology.
Facts.Fact 9: The patent filing highlighted the significance of cooling the material shortly after extrusion, in order to maintain the desired shape and structural integrity.
Facts.Fact 10: Scott Crump's early patents established the foundational aspects of FDM technology, contributing significantly to the development and popularization of 3D printing globally.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) was initially developed in the 1980s by Scott Crump, who later co-founded Stratasys Ltd., a leader in 3D printing technologies
Facts.Fact 2: The first material used in the FDM process was a plastic filament. This was due to the need for a material that could easily be extruded and that would cool and solidify quickly.
Facts.Fact 3: The original patent for FDM, submitted by Scott Crump in 1989, describes the use of thermoplastic polymer filament as the first material
Facts.Fact 4: Early FDM machines used thermoplastics such as acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polylactic acid (PLA), polycarbonate (PC), and high-density polyethylene (HDPE) as the primary materials for printing.
Facts.Fact 5: Some of the first materials used in FDM, like ABS plastic, were chosen because they could be heated to a semi-liquid state, extruded through a small nozzle, and then quickly cooled and hardened into a solid shape.
Facts.Fact 6: In the early years of FDM technology, filament-based materials were chosen due to their low cost and availability. As the technology evolved, more expensive engineering thermoplastics were introduced.
Facts.Fact 7: In the beginning, the filaments used in FDM were uniform in diameter. This consistency ensured that the 3D printer could accurately control the deposition of material, leading to better quality prints.
Facts.Fact 8: Initially, FDM materials lacked color diversity. Most of the early filaments were available only in natural or white-colored plastic, and it wasn't until later that a larger range of colors became available.
Facts.Fact 9: Another motivation for the first FDM materials was their environmental stability. Materials such as ABS and PLA are resistant to many environmental influences such as UV light and moisture, making them ideal for a vast range of applications.
Facts.Fact 10: In the early phase of FDM, the materials used were mainly chosen for their ease of processing and not for their mechanical properties. This changed over the years, leading to the use of materials like PEEK and ULTEM which provide superior mechanical strength but are more challenging to process.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a 3D printing technology first developed by Scott Crump in the 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: Crump filed a patent for FDM technology in the United States in 1989, under the name 'Apparatus and method for creating three-dimensional objects', which was awarded in November 1992.
Facts.Fact 3: In the process of FDM development, the concept of 'thermoplastic extrusion' was first coined, where a thermoplastic material is heated and extruded layer by layer to form an object.
Facts.Fact 4: The initial breakthrough of FDM technology was in getting precision in the layer-by-layer extrusion and cooling to create detailed models.
Facts.Fact 5: One significant technological breakthrough in FDM was the incorporation of dissolvable support structures which permit the creation of more complex models.

Facts.Fact 7: The introduction of heated print beds and closed build chambers were major technological enhancements that improved the quality and reliability of fused deposition modeling.
Facts.Fact 8: By the late 1990s, FDM technology became more accessible commercially with the launch of affordable 3D printers for the consumer market.
Facts.Fact 9: In 2005, the RepRap project led to a significant breakthrough in FDM technology by creating a self-replicating 3D printer, further lowering the barriers to entry for this technology.

Facts.Fact 9: The evolution of FDM technology also saw advancements in software algorithms which optimize the print process, improving accuracy and reducing material wastage.
Facts.Fact 10: In recent years, innovations in FDM technology have focused on enhancing its potential for mass production, with developments such as automated print farms where multiple prints can be managed simultaneously.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling was originally developed in the 1980s by Scott Crump, who later co-founded the company Stratasys. He advanced the technology by inventing a way to use thermoplastics, which was a significant material advancement in the evolution of FDM.
Facts.Fact 2: In late 1980s and early 1990s, materials primarily used in FDM were ABS, polycarbonate, and polyphenolsulfone. As the technology evolved, more materials became compatible with FDM.
Facts.Fact 3: Material advancements in fused deposition modeling have seen the introduction and enhanced usage of high-performance thermoplastics like ULTEM 9085 and ULTEM 1010 that offer heightened strength and thermal stability compared to earlier materials.
Facts.Fact 4: Advancements in materials for FDM led to increased possibilities in end-use applications. For instance, flexible materials like TPU 92A enable the production of parts that can bend or stretch without damage.
Facts.Fact 5: Companies like Stratasys have led the way in the development of new printing materials like Nylon12 Carbon Fiber, which is tougher, more versatile and can withstand higher temperatures than traditional FDM materials, broadening the scope of parts that can be 3D printed using FDM.
Facts.Fact 6: Further advancements in material technology introduced sophisticated fills such as chopped carbon fiber to the FDM process. This opened up high-performance applications in the automotive and aerospace industries among others.
Facts.Fact 7: Modern FDM technology also allows for the use of composite materials. This allows for lighter but durable parts, beneficial in industries like aerospace and medical.
Facts.Fact 8: In recent years, material advancements have led to the possibility of FDM with metal, known as 'Fused Filament Fabrication' (FFF). This is made possible by metal powders held in a filament matrix, which is sintered post-print.
Facts.Fact 9: The evolution of FDM materials has further seen the introduction of bio-compatible materials, now making it possible to create custom prosthetics and surgical aids with fused deposition modeling.
Facts.Fact 10: The increasingly eco-friendly bend of the industry has also seen material advancements in FDM, with an increasing use of sustainable, biodegradable materials like PLA (Polylactic Acid).

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was first developed by S. Scott Crump in the late 1980s. Crump later commercialized this technology through his company, Stratasys Ltd.
Facts.Fact 2: By the early 1990s, FDM technology had evolved and was used increasingly in additive manufacturing, a trend which led to significant hardware improvements. This included the development of larger print frames and enhanced nozzle designs for more precise product output.
Facts.Fact 3: In the mid-2000s, FDM hardware saw a wide-scale adaptation of multi-material printing capabilities. This allowed users to generate objects with different materials in a single print run, expanding the versatility and usefulness of FDM.
Facts.Fact 4: The advent of heated build platforms was another significant hardware evolution. In the beginning, FDM struggled with warping of materials during cooling; heated build platforms mitigated this issue, improving the final product's quality.
Facts.Fact 5: The evolution of FDM printers saw drastic improvement in resolution over time. Enhanced stepper motors and more accurate positioning systems led to an increase in the possible layer resolution from 250 micrometres to as low as 20 micrometres.
Facts.Fact 6: In the 2010s, the use of dual extruder systems was introduced. These system could print with two different materials simultaneously, drastically reducing the print time for complex objects and widening the range of possible applications for FDM technology.
Facts.Fact 7: There have been notable improvements in filament technologies over the years. This includes the development of a wide variety of filament materials from ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene) and PLA (Polylactic Acid) to exotic filaments like wood, metal, and thermochromic filaments.
Facts.Fact 8: Hardware advancements facilitated faster print speeds in FDM technology. Early FDM printers could only manage a speed of few millimeters per second, whereas modern FDM printers can reach speeds of up to 500 millimeters per second.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM printers' size became more compact over time due to better hardware design. While early machines were often large and unwieldy, modern personal FDM printers can fit on a desktop.
Facts.Fact 10: Direct Drive and Bowden tube extruder systems were significant improvements made on FDM printers. While Direct Drive extruders provide better control of the filament and allow for more detailed prints, Bowden tube extruders allow for higher printing speed and reduced printer size.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) technology was developed by S. Scott Crump in the late 1980s while the first commercial FDM machine, 'the 3D Modeler', was introduced by Stratasys Ltd. in 1992.
Facts.Fact 2: The original software used for FDM printers was proprietary, tied specifically to the hardware produced by Stratasys and consisting of specific machine commands.
Facts.Fact 3: Following the expiration of the FDM patent in 2009, the open-source 3D printing movement led to the development of non-proprietary software solutions for FDM, such as ReplicatorG and Slic3r.
Facts.Fact 4: ReplicatorG, developed in 2010, was one of the first open-source software for controlling 3D print preparation and the printer itself. It was primarily designed for the MakerBot, but also supports a wide range of 3D printers.
Facts.Fact 5: One significant advancement in FDM software was the introduction of slicers. These software programs, like Slic3r and Cura, interpret 3D models and translate them into layers for the printer to produce.
Facts.Fact 6: In 2012, the Ultimaker introduced Cura, a free slicer software that provides a seamless integration between 3D modeling and printing. It's famed for its user-friendly interface and high-quality print profiles.
Facts.Fact 7: In 2015, Autodesk developed Print Studio, a software catering to FDM printers, offering model repair and support generation, which was a significant progress in the capabilities of 3D printing software.
Facts.Fact 8: Cloud-based SaaS (Software as a Service) platforms like AstroPrint and 3DPrinterOS were developed for greater accessibility, allowing users to manage and monitor their FDM printers from any web-enabled device.
Facts.Fact 9: Recently, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) started to integrate into FDM software developments to analyze and optimize print settings and the behavior of materials during the print process.
Facts.Fact 10: Software has been developed to address specific industry needs, such as Materialise's Build Processor for complex professional printing, or dental-specific software like 3Shape, enhancing the usability of FDM printing in these fields.

Facts.Fact 1: The open-source movement transitioned Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) from a commercial to an accessible, community-driven technology.
Facts.Fact 2: The RepRap Project, initiated in 2005, was the first significant open-source initiative in FDM, aimed at creating a self-replicating machine.
Facts.Fact 3: In 2007, the first operational RepRap prototype successfully printed half of its own next version parts, marking a major milestone in the open-source movement.
Facts.Fact 4: By 2010, RepRap users had significantly increased, leading to the proliferation of open-source FDM technology worldwide.
Facts.Fact 5: The RepRap project resulted in the development of open-source software like Slic3r and Cura, which allowed users to manipulate digital models for FDM printing.
Facts.Fact 6: Open-source initiatives like the RepRap project led to a drop in the cost of FDM printers, making 3D printing technology more accessible to public.
Facts.Fact 7: The open-source movement encouraged the development of a multitude of FDM printer variations, resulting in printers like the Delta, Core XY, and H-Bot models.
Facts.Fact 8: Consumer-oriented FDM companies like Prusa Research and Ultimaker were born out of the open-source movement and continue to contribute to it.
Facts.Fact 9: In addition to hardware contributions, the open-source movement encouraged creation of a vast online database of printable 3D models such as Thingiverse, MyMiniFactory, and YouMagine.
Facts.Fact 10: The open-source movement in FDM led to an increase in innovation and quality, as communities were incentivized to improve upon and share their design alterations and optimizations.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM), was invented by Scott Crump, co-founder of Stratasys, Ltd., in the late 1980s - marking the inception of a novel manufacturing technology.
Facts.Fact 2: In 1992, Stratasys manufactured and sold the very first FDM machine (the '3D Modeler') which brought FDM technology to the market for broader accessibility.
Facts.Fact 3: Initially, FDM was marketed primarily towards rapid prototyping. The technology gained attention for its ability to create robust, functional prototypes in a variety of materials.
Facts.Fact 4: The global adoption of FDM really took off in the 2000s when the patent expired. The expiration allowed numerous companies to create their own versions of FDM 3D printers, promoting widespread dissemination of the technology.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM technology's popularity skyrocketed and eventually became the most widely used 3D printing technology globally, accounting for approximately 44% of the 3D printing market in 2018 according to a report by Sculpteo.
Facts.Fact 6: In 2009, the creation of RepRap - an open-source FDM 3D printer, significantly boosted the global adoption of FDM. This technology became the basis for many 3D printer models, including MakerBot and Ultimaker.
Facts.Fact 7: The versatility of FDM technology, printing with a wide range of thermoplastic materials, has championed its adoption in various industries including aerospace, automotive, healthcare, and education among others.
Facts.Fact 8: The evolution of FDM has led to the development of numerous specialty filaments, amplifying its utility. This includes flexible, soluble, conductive, and composite materials that have expanded possibilities for design and function.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM's lower costs, user-friendliness, and safety compared to other 3D printing technologies have played a significant part in its global adoption, making it a favourite for home and educational use.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM technology continues to evolve with recent advancements towards hybrid 3D printers, combining traditional FDM with other manufacturing processes like CNC machining and laser engraving, offering more capabilities to the users, pushing the boundaries of the global adoption of FDM.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) education integration began in the late 1980s and early 1990s, shortly after its invention by S. Scott Crump, initially being introduced in engineering and design programs.
Facts.Fact 2: The increasing affordability and accessibility of FDM machines have allowed many schools, from elementary to post-secondary, to implement 3D printers into their curriculum.
Facts.Fact 3: In many educational settings, FDM technology is used as a practical tool to introduce students to CAD software and rapid prototyping techniques, providing hands-on experience.
Facts.Fact 4: Some universities, such as Savannah College of Art and Design, have integrated FDM into their curriculum to give students the opportunity to create physical models of their designs.
Facts.Fact 5: The use of FDM in education promotes interdisciplinary learning, as it can be utilized by a range of subjects including engineering, design, art, science, and mathematics.
Facts.Fact 6: Educational integration of FDM has led to a rise in collaborative learning environments as it encourages students to work together on projects that require designing, prototyping, and iterative testing.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM technology has also entered extracurricular activities with many schools initiating 3D printing clubs or integrating it into existing tech clubs.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM's popularity in education has been practical in introducing students to environmental concepts, as the machines can use biodegradable thermoplastics.
Facts.Fact 9: Educational integration of FDM often includes teaching students about the implications of 3D printing in various industries, such as healthcare, manufacturing, and aerospace, preparing them for potential career paths.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM technology has seen utilization in remote education models, giving teachers unique ways to engage students with hands-on projects from home, a trend accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) was first developed in the late 1980s by S. Scott Crump, co-founder of Stratasys, Inc.
Facts.Fact 2: Crump patented the FDM technology in 1989, giving Stratasys the exclusive rights to its commercial use and marking a key milestone in FDM evolution and standardization.
Facts.Fact 3: Following the expiration of the initial FDM patent in 2009, many open-source 3D printers using FDM technology emerged, feeding into standardization efforts.
Facts.Fact 4: Efforts of standardization for FDM have been led by organizations such as the American Society for Testing Materials (ASTM) which introduced ASTM F2792, defining terms and processes in additive manufacturing, including FDM.
Facts.Fact 5: ISO/ASTM52900:2015 was another vital milestone in the standardization of FDM and related technologies, providing universally applicable terminologies and definitions.
Facts.Fact 6: The ASTM and ISO have also been working on a series of standards (ISO/ASTM 52910-52912, 52915-52920) specifically aimed at outlining the principles, aspects of the design, process and quality parameters, and testing methodologies for FDM and other 3D printing technologies.
Facts.Fact 7: The standardization process has been key in promoting the integration of FDM technologies into industries such as aerospace, automotive, and medicine by ensuring consistent process quality and results.
Facts.Fact 8: In the evolution of FDM, material standardization has been a critical aspect. Early FDM printers mostly used ABS plastic, but the range of materials has expanded to include PLA, nylon, and others, leading to the establishment of standardized guidelines for material usage.
Facts.Fact 9: Standardization has also covered the software aspect of FDM, with STL (Stereolithography) files being the universal standard for 3D printing, including FDM, paving the way towards the use of more advanced formats like 3MF and AMF.
Facts.Fact 10: In recent years, standardization efforts have focused on integrating FDM into digital manufacturing workflows, with standards for interconnecting software, hardware, and post-processing systems, and even assessing environmental impact, which is all significant evolution in the field of FDM.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) was invented in the late 1980s by S. Scott Crump and commercialized by Stratasys Ltd. in 1990s, after overcoming several technical and patent-related challenges.
Facts.Fact 2: In the early days, one of the significant challenges faced was achieving a precise and accurate control over the extrusion process of the filament which resulted in low quality output.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM had a major limitation in the early stages - limited material options. It initially only worked with thermoplastics, limiting its application in industries that required other materials.
Facts.Fact 4: Advancements with multi-material printing faced obstacles due to inconsistent extrusion rates among the materials causing problems in creating homogeneous multi-material parts.
Facts.Fact 5: During FDM's evolution, another challenge was in scaling up the technology for industrial applications. The size of components that could be produced was limited based on the capacity of the FDM machine.
Facts.Fact 6: In the initial stage of FDM development, it faced the challenge of slow print speed. This was a significant hurdle for industries where production speed was a critical factor.
Facts.Fact 7: Overcoming post-processing complications was another challenge in the evolution of FDM. Removal of support structures and improving surface finish required additional efforts and time.
Facts.Fact 8: In terms of eco-friendliness, FDM faced challenges associated with waste generation. Unlike other additive manufacturing techniques, the FDM process generates plastic waste that poses environmental challenges.
Facts.Fact 9: Securing intellectual property rights emerged as a significant issue in FDM's history. It was challenging to obtain and maintain the exclusive rights to the technology, especially with numerous similar patents in existence.
Facts.Fact 10: A significant challenge for FDM was inducing anisotropy in the printed components caused by layer-wise fabrication. This led to variations in mechanical properties depending on the orientation of the printed part.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling technology was developed and patented by S. Scott Crump, co-founder of Stratasys Ltd., in the late 1980s.
Facts.Fact 2: Stratasys launched the first FDM 3D printer in 1991, marking the beginning of the market growth phase for this technology.
Facts.Fact 3: From 1995 to 2005, the Fused Deposition Modeling market expanded as more companies started producing FDM machines with industrial-grade capabilities.
Facts.Fact 4: In 2005, Stratasys released the 'Dimension' series, which was aimed at providing affordable, office-friendly FDM 3D printers. This helped to democratize the technology and significantly boosted its market growth.
Facts.Fact 5: The early 2010s saw an explosion in the consumer market for FDM 3D printers, driven by the expiration of key parts of the FDM patent in 2009. The expired patents allowed new companies to produce and sell cheap FDM machines, thus accelerating market growth.
Facts.Fact 6: By 2015, FDM technology held the largest share of the 3D printing market, demonstrating its popularity and rapid adoption across various industries.
Facts.Fact 7: As further evidence of market growth, the global FDM 3D printer market was estimated to be valued at $3.3 billion by the end of 2018.
Facts.Fact 8: The FDM market continues to grow at an exponential rate, with a predicted total value of $12.4 billion by 2027, according to a report published by Forencis Research (2020).
Facts.Fact 9: Spurred by market growth, the evolution of FDM technology has led to improvements in speed, precision, and material versatility, thereby increasing its applications in sectors such as healthcare, aerospace, and automotive.
Facts.Fact 10: In recent years, key players in the market, such as Stratasys, have been focusing on producing FDM machines with high-performance material capabilities, further advancing the technology and opening new commercial opportunities, thus fueling market growth.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) hardware primarily consists of a printing nozzle, build platform, filament feeding system and modeling software.
Facts.Fact 2: The filament feeding system in FDM hardware uses thermoplastic material, which is heated to its melting point and then extruded through a nozzle.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM hardware often uses roll-type thermoplastic material, which differs from other 3D printing technology that uses powder or liquid resin.
Facts.Fact 4: Most FDM printers have a single nozzle, but some advanced models possess dual nozzles that can print with two different types of filament, or two colors.
Facts.Fact 5: The build platform in FDM hardware, also known as the print bed, is typically heated. This feature helps prevent the bottom layer of the model from warping due to cooling.
Facts.Fact 6: The directional accuracy of FDM hardware is controlled along the three Cartesian axes (X, Y, and Z). This makes FDM technology a type of Cartesian 3D print technology.
Facts.Fact 7: The software used in FDM hardware includes slicing software that transforms digital 3D models into a series of thin layers, creating a toolpath for the extruder.
Facts.Fact 8: Modern FDM hardware may include automatic filament feed systems, and some can even sense when filament runs out and pause the printing process until it is replaced.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM printers hardware has different resolutions, typically measured in microns (µm). The layer height commonly ranges from 100 (high resolution) to 300 microns (low resolution).
Facts.Fact 10: A unique characteristic of FDM hardware is its ability to create part with complex geometries and cavities using dissolvable support structures made from different filament material.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) printers create objects by extruding plastic material, typically in the form of a filament, layer by layer.
Facts.Fact 2: Within FDM printers, there's a specific part called an extruder, which is responsible for melting the filament and depositing it onto the print bed. It includes two sub-parts: a 'hot end', where the actual melting occurs, and a 'cold end', which pushes the filament into the hot end.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM printers typically use materials like ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene) or PLA (Polylactic Acid) filaments due to their ideal thermal properties, cost-effectiveness, and ease of use.
Facts.Fact 4: One of the pieces of hardware present in FDM printers is the build platform. The design and surface of the build platform can directly influence the outcome's adhesion and precision.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM printers can incorporate dual-extruder systems, allowing for the simultaneous use of two different types of filament material or two different colors of the same material.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM printers use stepper motors to control the precise movements of the extruder and the build platform in the X, Y, and Z axes.
Facts.Fact 7: FDM printers often include a heated build platform, which is fundamental to prevent warping and to enhance adhesion of the first layer of the print to the build surface.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM printers can offer a varying degree of print resolution based on layer thickness. Lower layers (from 50 to 200 microns, for instance) offer high resolution but may require more time to print.
Facts.Fact 9: The nozzle diameter in FDM printers impacts the print quality and speed. Nozzles with smaller diameters provide high-detail prints but slower printing times, whereas larger nozzles offer faster printing times but lower quality.
Facts.Fact 10: Some high-end FDM printers feature enclosures. Enclosed printing spaces help maintain a constant temperature around the print, aiding in the quality of some prints and allowing the use of more heat-sensitive materials.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) desktop printers utilize a thermoplastic filament, which is heated to its melting point and then extruded, layer by layer, to create a three-dimensional object.
Facts.Fact 2: Most FDM desktop models offer a printing resolution range between 50 to 100 microns, although printers with higher resolution capabilities are also available.
Facts.Fact 3: Common materials used by FDM desktop printers include ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene) and PLA (Polylactic Acid), both of which have unique benefits and trade-offs.
Facts.Fact 4: User-friendly software interfaces are a notable feature in FDM desktop printers. Many use slicing software, which converts a digital 3D model into readable instructions for the printer.
Facts.Fact 5: Due to their compact size, FDM desktop models often have a smaller build volume compared to their larger, industrial counterparts. They are typically designed to fit comfortably in office or home environments.
Facts.Fact 6: Desktop FDM printers such as the MakerBot Replicator and Ultimaker 2+ have gained popularity due to their reliability, precision, and relative ease of use.
Facts.Fact 7: Some FDM desktop printers are equipped with dual extrusion capabilities, allowing them to print in multiple colors or materials simultaneously.
Facts.Fact 8: Latest FDM desktop models incorporate features like automatic bed leveling and filament detection for enhanced printing experience and are also becoming increasingly connected, with Wi-Fi and cloud-based capabilities.
Facts.Fact 9: Desktop FDM printers are often used in prototyping and educational environments due to their affordable price point and simplicity of operation.
Facts.Fact 10: Due to their open-source nature, many desktop FDM printers can be modified and upgraded by users for enhanced performance or to meet specific printing needs.

Facts.Fact 1: Industrial FDM printers often feature multiple print heads, which lets them produce objects with more than one material or color.
Facts.Fact 2: Unlike some consumer-grade models, industrial FDM printers use high-performance thermoplastics for improved durability and heat resistance in the final product.
Facts.Fact 3: They can print parts of significant size, due to their larger build volume compared to desktop models.
Facts.Fact 4: Advanced temperature control on industrial FDM printers provides greater precision during printing, reducing errors and improving final product quality.
Facts.Fact 5: Some industrial models of FDM printers have the capability to dissolve support structures in a water-based solution, minimizing the need for manual post-processing.
Facts.Fact 6: Industrial FDM printers have in-built quality assessment tools, which can automatically detect and rectify errors, increasing the overall success rate of prints.
Facts.Fact 7: They use enclosed build chambers to maintain a controlled environment, reducing the risk of warping or deformation due to external conditions like temperature and humidity changes.
Facts.Fact 8: Many industrial models have networking capabilities, allowing them to be integrated into a production line or managed remotely for increased efficiency and productivity.
Facts.Fact 9: Industrial FDM printers are often used in industries such as automotive and aerospace due to their ability to produce strong, durable parts, and their compatibility with materials used in these sectors.
Facts.Fact 10: While industrial FDM printers have a high initial cost, their long-term durability, speed, and efficiency often prove more cost-effective for businesses in the long run.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) printers are highly customizable, with a variety of options for altering structure and functionality.
Facts.Fact 2: Customization can range from simple modifications, such as altering the printer's aesthetic design, to more complex adjustments like improving print speed or precision.
Facts.Fact 3: The extruder, which is the component that melts and deposits the filament, can be customized to support different types and diameters of filament material, thus expanding the range of printable objects.
Facts.Fact 4: The build plate of an FDM printer can be upgraded, not only to increase print size capacity, but also to improve the surface quality of the printed objects.
Facts.Fact 5: Users can use open-source software to tinker with the CNC controller of their FDM printer, which controls the printer's movement and extrusion. This allows for deeper customization compared to proprietary software.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM printers' print resolution, which affects the fineness and detail of printed objects, can be customized by changing the type and size of the printer's nozzle.
Facts.Fact 7: The cooling system of an FDM printer, which affects processing time and finish quality, can be customized to offer optimal cooling and reduced warping.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM printers can be fitted with dual extruders, allowing them to print objects with multiple materials or colors.
Facts.Fact 9: Customizable features also extend to the printer's user interface, including the addition of touchscreens or the use of custom control software.
Facts.Fact 10: To improve print speed and reduce noise, some users customize their FDM printers with upgraded stepper motors, like those designed for quieter operation and greater torque.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) printers feature automated bed leveling, a feature which aids in ensuring the print bed is flat and aligned, improving the overall print quality.
Facts.Fact 2: Most FDM 3D printers are equipped with filament detection capabilities. This automated feature allows the printer to pause printing when it runs out of filament, preventing incomplete prints.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM printers often come with power resume functions, an automation feature that allows the printer to record the last known position and resume printing after power loss.
Facts.Fact 4: Many FDM printers incorporate software enhancements like slicers which allow automated conversion of STL, OBJ, and other 3D graphics files into G-code, the language that the 3D printer understands.
Facts.Fact 5: Automation in FDM printers includes real-time monitoring, which helps in tracking the performance of the printer and troubleshooting potential issues instantly.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM printers have integrated cooling systems that automatically switch on or off to control the temperature during the print job, ensuring the filament solidifies at the desired rate and preventing print deformities.
Facts.Fact 7: Some FDM printers feature automated cleaning mechanisms that ensure the print nozzle is kept clear, reducing the risk of clogging and improving print reliability.
Facts.Fact 8: Advancements in FDM printer automation have led to the development of multi-material printing, allowing automated switches between different filament types or colors during a single print job.
Facts.Fact 9: Certain FDM printers offer cloud-based Wi-Fi connectivity that allows for automated control and monitoring of print jobs remotely – an integral feature for industrial applications.
Facts.Fact 10: Many high-end FDM printers include automated calibration features such as Z-probing and mesh bed leveling, making the setup process simpler and reducing the need for manual intervention.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) printers use a variety of sensors to monitor and control the printing process.
Facts.Fact 2: Thermal sensors on FDM printers monitor the temperature of the printer head to ensure that thermoplastic materials are at the correct heat for extrusion.
Facts.Fact 3: Some FDM printers have filament presence sensors. These sensors detect if the filament has run out or broken, pausing the print so filament can be reloaded.
Facts.Fact 4: FDM printers use optical sensors for bed leveling, a critical step in the 3D printing process. These sensors ensure that the print bed is even before printing begins.
Facts.Fact 5: Proximity sensors on FDM printers can detect potential collisions with the printer head, helping to prevent damage and misprints.
Facts.Fact 6: FDM printers often feature humidity sensors, as the quality of a 3D print can get severely impacted by high levels of humidity. These sensors help to monitor the storage environment of the filament.
Facts.Fact 7: Many FDM printers integrate with motion sensors, which facilitate precise movement and placement of the printer head. This contributes to the accuracy and fidelity of the final print.
Facts.Fact 8: On advanced FDM printers, pressure sensors within the extruder can detect clogs or obstructions, alerting the user to the issue before it causes a print failure.
Facts.Fact 9: Some high-end FDM printers have integrated camera sensors to visually monitor the printing process, enabling the users to catch any issues in real-time, or even watch their design come to life remotely.
Facts.Fact 10: FDM printers can include calibration sensors, used to calibrate the device to ensure accurate prints. These sensors primarily check the alignment and spacing of printer components.

Facts.Fact 1: Routine cleaning is crucial for FDM printers to remove any residual filament from the nozzle which can obstruct the flow of the filament and compromise the quality of the print.
Facts.Fact 2: Maintenance often includes calibrating the print bed to ensure that it is level - an uneven print bed can lead to misprints or damage to the printer itself.
Facts.Fact 3: Replacing worn-out parts in a timely manner is a key area of FDM printer maintenance. This can include components such as belts, extruders, or fans.
Facts.Fact 4: Printers that use Fused Deposition Modeling technology require firmware updates regularly. These updates often include performance improvements, new features, and bug fixes.
Facts.Fact 5: Periodical lubrication of the moving parts is essential for the FDM printer to function smoothly. This can include rods, bearings, and any other mechanisms that move during operation.
Facts.Fact 6: Maintenance of FDM printers includes monitoring and replacing the BuildTak surface or similar build surfaces when they show signs of wear. This helps ensure optimal adhesion during printing.
Facts.Fact 7: Regular inspection of the drive gears in an FDM printer is recommended as filament dust can clog the gears over time, leading to under-extrusion or, in severe cases, filament grinding.
Facts.Fact 8: Ensuring adequate ventilation for the printer is part of its maintenance. Some materials used in FDM printing can release fumes that may be harmful if inhaled in large quantities.
Facts.Fact 9: Storage of filaments is also a crucial aspect of FDM printer maintenance. Improper storage can lead to moisture absorption leading to suboptimal print quality.
Facts.Fact 10: Checking the electrical connections and wiring should be conducted during maintenance as with time and usage, they can loosen or wear which can affect the printer's performance.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) printers use thermoplastic filament. This filament is heated and extruded through a nozzle, creating layers, which subsequent layers are built upon.
Facts.Fact 2: The layer resolution of FDM printers is an essential performance metric. It effectively communicates the thinness of the layers in a print, and is typically measured in microns. The smaller the value, the higher the resolution.
Facts.Fact 3: FDM printers' speed, measured in millimeters per second (mm/s), is a performance determinant. Faster print speeds could sometimes compromise on print quality.
Facts.Fact 4: The ability to utilize various materials, like ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene), PLA (Polylactic Acid), Nylon, etc., expands the versatility of FDM printers.
Facts.Fact 5: FDM Printers' build volume, measured in cubic inches or millimeters, is another performance metric. It indicates the maximum size of an object that can be printed.
Facts.Fact 6: The nozzle diameter of FDM printers can impact the print resolution and speed. A smaller nozzle provides high-resolution prints but reduces printing speed.
Facts.Fact 7: Extruder quality is a pivotal metric within printer performance. Extruders with advanced features can handle a wider range of filament types and diameters, which in turn, affects print quality.
Facts.Fact 8: The performance of an FDM printer can be influenced by software compatibility. Most FDM printers work with any 3D slicing software, but some printers work best with proprietary software.
Facts.Fact 9: FDM printers' stability and rigidity also play role in print results. A stable frame reduces vibration during printing, leading to better print quality.
Facts.Fact 10: Capability of a heated print bed is another performance area to consider, as it helps reduce warping in print materials and aids in better adhesion of the first layer.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) printers are becoming increasingly more accessible to a wider audience as prices have significantly decreased in recent years.
Facts.Fact 2: Many FDM printers have user-friendly interfaces, often including touchscreen controls, which make them more accessible for users with varying levels of technological experience.
Facts.Fact 3: The open-source movement in the 3D printing industry has improved accessibility by promoting the development of affordable, DIY FDM printers.
Facts.Fact 4: FDM printers support a variety of materials such as PLA, ABS, and PETG, making them accessible for a range of applications and user requirements.
Facts.Fact 5: The modularity of some FDM printers allows users to upgrade or replace components, enhancing longevity and overall access to evolving technologies.
Facts.Fact 6: Accessible software options for FDM printers range from entry-level solutions with basic features to more advanced software providing detailed control for experienced users.
Facts.Fact 7: Some FDM printers feature automatic leveling, removing the need for manual calibration and making the technology more accessible for novice users.
Facts.Fact 8: FDM printers are available in a variety of sizes to fit different spaces and production needs, allowing accessibility in both personal and professional environments.
Facts.Fact 9: Online communities and resources have made FDM printers more accessible by providing user support and troubleshooting advice.
Facts.Fact 10: Many manufacturers of FDM printers offer technical support and comprehensive warranty packages, ensuring accessibility through reliable service coverage.

Facts.Fact 1: Entry-level FDM printers are typically priced between $200 and $500, making them relatively affordable for hobbyists and newcomers to 3D printing.
Facts.Fact 2: Mid-range FDM printers can cost anywhere from $500 to $3000, offering improved print quality and reliability over entry-level models.
Facts.Fact 3: High-end FDM printers, favored by professionals and commercial users, typically range in price from $3,000 up to $20,000 or more.
Facts.Fact 4: FDM printers in the higher price ranges often have advanced features such as larger build volumes, dual-extruder capabilities, and enclosed printing environments.
Facts.Fact 5: Certain high-priced FDM printers also offer multi-material printing capabilities, which significantly expands the possibilities for final print designs.
Facts.Fact 6: The cost of FDM printers can also be determined by the brand, with industry-leading brands like MakerBot and Ultimaker demanding higher prices due to their reputation for quality and reliability.
Facts.Fact 7: Though the initial cost is an important factor, potential buyers should also consider the ongoing cost of filament, which can vary depending on the quality, type of material, and brand.
Facts.Fact 8: Affordable FDM printers may require additional post-processing of prints or adjustments for optimal performance, consequently leading to a potential hidden cost in terms of time and labor.
Facts.Fact 9: Educational and institutional packages, which often come with multiple FDM printers, pre-installed software, and support, can range from $5,000 to upwards of $50,000.
Facts.Fact 10: Some high-end FDM printers also incorporate smart features, such as remote monitoring or automated calibration systems, contributing to their higher price range.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused deposition modeling (FDM) was first developed by a company named Stratasys, founded by S. Scott Crump in the late 80s. Stratasys remains one of the leading manufacturers of FDM printers today.
Facts.Fact 2: Ultimaker, a Dutch manufacturer, is highly reputed for producing FDM printers that deliver top-notch print quality and have excellent software and community support.
Facts.Fact 3: MakerBot is a Brooklyn, New York-based company that manufactures FDM printers. MakerBot gained acclaim with their Replicator and Thing-o-Matic series of printers.
Facts.Fact 4: Prusa Research is a Czech company that manufactures FDM printers. They are well regarded for their open-source approach and their Prusa i3 printer, loved by the maker community.
Facts.Fact 5: German manufacturer, Wanhao, is known for creating affordable, user-friendly FDM printers for entry-level users and educational environments.
Facts.Fact 6: Fortus is a high-performance line of FDM printers designed for industrial use by Stratasys. The Fortus printers can work with a wide range of thermoplastic materials for diverse manufacturing needs.
Facts.Fact 7: Creality is a Chinese manufacturer known for their popular Ender and CR series of budget-oriented FDM printers.
Facts.Fact 8: Anycubic, another Chinese manufacturer, produces FDM printers that are appreciated for their accuracy and reliability.
Facts.Fact 9: Italian manufacturer Roboze specializes in FDM printers designed for high-performance materials, capable of handling super polymers and composites.
Facts.Fact 10: American manufacturer LulzBot, a brand by Aleph Objects, develops FDM printers focused on customization and resilience, popular for their TAZ and Mini printers.

Facts.Fact 1: Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) hardware consists of various components, including a 3D printing nozzle, filament, stepper motors, belts, extruders, power supply unit, and a controller board.
Facts.Fact 2: The 3D printing nozzle is primarily responsible for depositing the molten filament onto the print bed. The size of the nozzle dictates the resolution of the FDM 3D prints with typical sizes ranging between 0.1 mm and 0.5 mm.
Facts.Fact 3: The Filament in FDM printers serve as a material source. These filaments come in several materials like PLA (Polylactic Acid), ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene), and PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol), with various diameters ranging from 1.75 millimeters to 3.00 millimeters.
Facts.Fact 4: Stepper Motors play a crucial role in FDM printers because they move the print head and bed. The precision and speed of these motors directly affect the print quality.
Facts.Fact 5: Belts in FDM printers are used to transmit the motion from the stepper motors to the movable parts of the printer. They are typically made of a rubber-like material reinforced with fiberglass or steel.
Facts.Fact 6: The extruder of an FDM printer has an essential role, heating and pushing the filament through the nozzle. It comprises two parts: a cold part (feeder) and a hot part (heater block and nozzle).
Facts.Fact 7: The power supply unit of an FDM printer offers the needed electrical energy for the printer to function. It's essential to choose one with appropriate voltage and current ratings to ensure system stability and safety.
